units.summary: Rabban Gamliel's court votes to nullify early Sabbatical year plowing restrictions, leading to a later exchange where Rabbi Abbahu is momentarily stunned by a challenge to the court's authority before providing a justification.
While walking along a road, Ravina and Rabba Tosefa’a witness a man drawing water on the intermediate days of a Festival, leading Rabba Tosefa’a to suggest he be excommunicated.
Following their encounter with a man drawing water, Ravina challenges Rabba Tosefa’a’s call for excommunication with a baraita, leading Rabba Tosefa’a to retract his statement.
Rav Yehuda permits the family of bar Tzitai to construct circular ditches for their vineyards on the intermediate days of a Festival.
A series of reports where Abaye, Rabbi Yirmeya, and Rav Ashi permit different communities to clear or dredge rivers during the Festival.
A student of Rabbi Yannai who usually challenged him daily refrained from doing so during public Festival lectures to avoid potentially embarrassing his teacher.
A man's savings for the pilgrimage to Jerusalem were given away by his wife to a professional eulogizer, preventing him from making the journey.
After two disciples return to take leave of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai a second time because they stayed in the city overnight, he sends his son to receive a blessing from them.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai sends his son to receive blessings from two sages, but their cryptic language causes the son distress until his father interprets them as profound blessings.
Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta is sent by his father to get a blessing from Rav, which his father later explains is a very great blessing based on biblical verses.
Rav Ḥisda's wife adorns herself on the Festival, leading to a sharp exchange between Rav Ḥisda and Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana regarding whether old women may use cosmetics.
Rav Beivai successfully beautifies his daughter with lime applied gradually, but a gentile neighbor who tries to do the same all at once accidentally kills his own daughter.
Rav Huna hears a man chiseling a millstone on the Festival and curses him for desecrating the day.
Ravina delayed a business sale during the festival and subsequently doubled his profit.
Ravina consulted Rav Ashi about collecting a debt from the people of Shanvata during the festival, and Rav Ashi permitted it because the debtors were currently available.
When the Bedita River overflowed and left fish stranded, the people gathered them and Rava permitted salting them to prevent loss.
Rava visited the Exilarch's house where they prepared fish for him by pressing it sixty times, and he ate it.
Rav visited Rav Shapir and was served a fish prepared in three distinct ways.
Mar son of Rav Aḥa, upon entering mourning, physically detached his ox from a shared team with Maryon son of Ravin, causing a work stoppage and financial loss.
Rav Safra and Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana refused to enter Mar Zutra's new mansion because it had been built by gentile contractors on Shabbat.
Rav Ḥama permitted the Exilarch's bath attendants to work on the intermediate days of a festival.
Rav Huna has his crops harvested on the Festival, leading his son to challenge the legality of the act based on a baraita.
Rav harvests his crop on the Festival, causing Shmuel to become angry until the circumstances are clarified.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia performs two controversial actions on Shabbat, leading Rabbi Ami to express dismay.
Passage B describes a specific action (chopping a palm tree) and a distinct narrative response (Abaye's curse), which constitutes a separate event from the previous passage.
Rav Ashi goes to cut his forest on the Festival and is questioned by Rav Sheila on his legal reasoning.
After Rabbi Yannai harvested his orchard on the Festival due to potential loss, the public began to do so habitually, leading Yannai to declare his orchard ownerless as a deterrent.
Rav Yosef moves wooden beams into his house during the day on the Festival, defending the lack of 'discretion' to Abaye by explaining the logistical difficulty of moving them at night.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira a hypothetical question about whether the sons of a man who died after planning to work on the Festival are penalized.
Rav Pappa recalls how Rava tested his students with a contradiction between two mishnayot regarding bringing tools from a craftsman, and how they successfully answered him.
Rav Huna permits spice merchants to sell in the market during the intermediate days of the festival, which Rav Kahana then challenges with a baraita.
A butcher is ostracized for insulting Rav Tuvi bar Mattana, later appeases him, leading Abaye to seek a method for lifting the ban.
After Bar Kappara makes a remark that offends Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Nasi snubbs him, leading Bar Kappara to treat himself as being under admonition.

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decrees that Torah should no longer be taught in the marketplace, based on his interpretation of Song of Songs. Rabbi Ḥiyya defies Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's decree against teaching in the marketplace, leading to a period of admonition and a subsequent confrontation where they debate the biblical merits of their positions.
Mar Ukva, distracted by a legal case, fails to honor Shmuel as usual, leading Shmuel to rebuke him in a way that the Gemara defines as a one-day admonition.
A woman refuses to move her leg for a passing scholar and is subsequently told by Rav Naḥman that the scholar's rebuke has placed her under admonition for one day.
Rav Yehuda excommunicates a scholar of ill repute, and despite the scholar's attempts to be released after Rav Yehuda's death, divine providence leads to his death by a wasp and a miraculous burial.
The maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi excommunicates a man she sees striking his adult son.
Reish Lakish excommunicates a man for stealing figs, but the man excommunicates him back, and the Sages rule that only the man's ban is valid, forcing Reish Lakish to seek a remedy.
A dog that ate the Sages' shoes was excommunicated, resulting in its tail catching fire.

A scholar harassed by a violent man seeks advice from Rav Yosef, who instructs him to perform a ritual with a written ban in a jug to avoid direct confrontation. Following Rav Yosef's advice, a scholar places a written ban in a jug in a cemetery and sounds shofars, resulting in the jug bursting and the death of his harasser.
When Shmuel questions his mourning brother Pineḥas about his long nails, Pineḥas's defensive reply inadvertently causes a bereavement for Shmuel himself.
Rav Shemen bar Abba observes Rabbi Yoḥanan cutting and discarding his nails in the study hall during the Festival.
Two sages ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi for a ruling on cutting nails during mourning.
Bar Hedya reports witnessing people laundering basins of linen garments in the Sea of Galilee during the intermediate days of the Festival.
Rava overhears a man praying to marry a specific woman and intervenes to tell him that such prayer is unnecessary if it is decreed and futile if it is not.
Rav Neḥemya reports finding Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa sitting together and ruling in accordance with Rav Huna.
Ravina arrives in Sura and is asked a legal question by Rav Chaviva regarding the duration of mourning.
Rav Hanina and Rav Natan bar Ami receive news of deaths and consult rabbis for the legal procedure regarding mourning.
Rabbi Tzadok learns of his father's death three years after the fact and consults Elisha ben Avuya on how to observe mourning.

Rav travels to Eretz Yisrael and engages in a coded dialogue with his uncle Rabbi Hiyya to discover if his parents are still alive. Rav and Rabbi Ḥiyya engage in a coded dialogue about the death of their relatives, leading Rabbi Ḥiyya to realize his siblings have died and immediately begin mourning rituals.
When Mar Ukva attempts to observe a full mourning period for his brother-in-law, Rav Huna enters and informs him that such mourning is only required for a father-in-law or mother-in-law.
After his grandson dies, Ameimar rends his garment several times, eventually standing up to re-do the act when he realizes the halakha requires rending while standing.
Passage B contains a distinct incident involving Rabbi Yosei in Tzippori that serves as a precedent for the legal ruling, separate from the incident involving Rabba bar bar Hana in Passage A.
When Rabba bar bar Hana was in mourning and considered canceling his lecture, Rabbi Hanina encouraged him to teach for the public's sake, leading him to seek an alternative method.
Following the death of his son, Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai entered the study hall and taught through Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya, who whispered his words to the public.
When Rabbi Akiva's sons died and a large crowd came to eulogize them, he stood on a bench and publicly thanked them, stating that the honor shown to his sons provided him consolation.
An anonymous student travels from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael to verify a legal tradition with Rabbi Abba, only to be told the tradition was reported incorrectly.
An incident is recounted where a leading sage refrained from removing his garment in mourning for his father because another sage intended to do the same out of respect.
Upon the death of the Nasi, Rav Hisda instructed Rav Hanan bar Rava to stand on a mortar and display his rent garment to the public.
Yosef the Priest's wife died, and he immediately proposed to her sister at the cemetery to care for the children, marrying her quickly but delaying intimacy.
Abaye and Rava wore specific types of clothing during their mourning periods to reflect different legal opinions.
A man who violated the prohibition against sexual relations during mourning was punished by having pigs drag his corpse.
Upon hearing of Rav's death, Shmuel performed an extreme act of mourning by rending twelve garments.
Abaye observes Rav Yosef practicing mourning rites privately on Shabbat and questions him about the legality of the act.
Rabbi Anani bar Sason teaches a law about mourning at the Nasi's house, causing Rabbi Ammi to become angry that he did not attribute the source.
Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa teaches a law in the Exilarch's pavilion, leading Rav Sheshet to express anger over the lack of attribution.

It describes a specific public event where Rav Pappa authorized Rav Avya the Elder to teach a ruling, followed by a specific response from Ravina, which constitutes a narrated incident distinct from the later encounter in Sura.
Ravina travels to Sura and is questioned by Rav Haviva regarding a ruling he reportedly gave about mourning before Rosh HaShana.
When Rav Safra died, the Sages initially refused to rend their garments because they weren't his students, but Abaye rebuked them and proved they were obligated to do so during the eulogy.
During Rav Huna's funeral, Rav Hisda manages several logistical and halakhic crises regarding the bier, and later rebukes his son for interrupting a eulogy with a question.
When Rav Huna's body was brought to Eretz Yisrael, Rav Hagga placed him in Rabbi Hiyya's cave, where the deceased sons of Rabbi Hiyya miraculously moved to make room for him.
At Rav Hisda's funeral, Rabbi Yitzhak prevented the Sages from placing a Torah on the bier and provided instructions on when to sew their mourning tears.

Rabba bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna died and were transported to Eretz Yisrael for burial. The bodies of Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rav Hamnuna are brought to Eretz Yisrael, causing camels to stop in honor and a child in Tiberias to deliver a poetic eulogy.
Passage B introduces a new protagonist (Ravina) and a distinct eulogy event, following the same literary form as the previous incident but independent of its narrative arc.
Rav Ashi, offended by the metaphors chosen by two eulogizers for Ravina's future funeral, becomes angry, causing their feet to become physically deformed.
When Rava feared the waters of the Tigris, he had Bar Avin recite a prayer for their safety.
Rabbi Hanin prayed for a child and died on the very day his son was born, leading to a poignant eulogy.
Passage B describes a distinct event involving different actors (Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar) and a specific eulogy, following the same structural form as Passage A.
Following the death of Rabbi Yoḥanan, Rabbi Ami observed an extended mourning period, which Rabbi Abba noted was a personal stringency rather than the law.
Passage B describes a distinct event involving the death and eulogy of Rabbi Zeira, featuring different actors and a different narrative focus than the mourning of Rabbi Yoḥanan in Passage A.

While Rabbi Abba was relieving himself, an ostrich nearly swallowed his phylacteries, leading him to seek a ruling from Rav Mattana and Rav Yehuda on the requirements for rending garments over damaged sacred texts.
When Rava was in mourning, Abba bar Marta visited him and overturned Rava's bed to demonstrate their closeness, leading Rava to comment on his behavior.
When Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua each gave instructions to overturn the beds at different stages of the funeral procession.
When Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael, Rav Tahalifa met him in the leather market and defined a 'dargash' for him.
The Gemara lists a series of communal enactments (Takkanot) made to prevent the poor from being embarrassed during funeral rites.
To stop the poor from abandoning their dead due to the high cost of shrouds, Rabban Gamliel modeled simplicity by being buried in plain linen, which became the new standard.
Rav Hamnuna arrived in a town and excommunicated the residents when he saw them working while a deceased person remained unburied.
A neighbor of Rav Huna ignored his warnings against excessive mourning for her son, resulting in the death of her remaining six sons and eventually herself.
Rav Yosef celebrates reaching age sixty to mark his escape from the punishment of karet, but Abaye reminds him that he is still subject to the 'karet of days.'
Following the sudden death of Rav Huna, the Sages are concerned until Zuga explains that sudden death is only a bad sign for those who haven't reached old age.
Rav Seorim watches his brother Rava die, and Rava later appears to him to describe the painless nature of his passing.
Rava attends the death of Rav Nachman and later receives a visit from him in a dream where Rav Nachman describes death as being as easy as removing a hair from milk.
Rabbi Elazar successfully argues with the Angel of Death to delay his death because he is currently eating sacred teruma.
Rav Sheshet encounters the Angel of Death in the market and convinces him to come to his home so he does not die like an animal in the street.
Rav Ashi convinces the Angel of Death to give him thirty days to review his learning before taking his soul.
The Angel of Death, unable to take Rav Chisda while he is studying, breaks a cedar column to startle him into silence so he can take his soul.
The Angel of Death disguises himself as a beggar to trick the righteous Rabbi Chiyya into a moment of vulnerability so he can take his soul.
When Rabbi Yishmael's sons died, four prominent sages visited him and delivered a series of comforting homilies after he first opened the conversation.
